walking-meeting-assistant.title: Turn a Screen-Free Meeting Into a Walking Meeting
walking-meeting-assistant.subtitle: Walk the meeting when the work can travel
walking-meeting-assistant.description: Use a walking meeting to replace part of a long sitting block when the conversation does not require a screen. Evidence supports the movement break, not a special meeting effect.
walking-meeting-assistant.reason: Replace an inherited walking-meeting article containing unsupported cognition percentages, step and heart-rate estimates, wind and battery pseudo-precision, and overbroad cardiometabolic claims. Two full-text 2026 systematic reviews/meta-analyses support a narrower claim: in acute controlled settings, interrupting prolonged sitting with physical activity, especially walking or light-to-moderate movement, improves postprandial glucose and insulin outcomes. The evidence does not test walking meetings as a format, establish a universal timer, or show long-term disease prevention.

lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: When a meeting is mostly listening and talking, replace some of that sitting with an easy walk if the route, weather, privacy and meeting format make it safe. Keep screen-heavy or safety-critical conversations seated. Capture decisions before you finish.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I replace a sitting block with walking without making the meeting worse? Was the route safe and the conversation easy enough to follow? Would I use this format again for this kind of meeting?
lifeOsSource.reference: Vanherle J, Franssen GHLM, Ivanova A, Eijnde BO, Franssen WMA. European Journal of Preventive Cardiology. 1 April 2026. Systematic review and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials.

faq.question: Do walking meetings have a special productivity or creativity effect?
faq.answer: This protocol does not claim that. The reviewed 2026 evidence is about the acute cardiometabolic effect of replacing prolonged sitting with physical activity. It did not test walking meetings as a meeting format, decision tool or creativity intervention.

faq.question: Should I set an alarm every 20 minutes?
faq.answer: Not as a universal rule. One 2026 meta-analysis found larger acute glucose and insulin reductions in studies using more frequent breaks, and a second review also found glucose benefited from frequent activity. But these were mostly short laboratory experiments with varied protocols. Twenty minutes is a research signal, not a law of office physiology.

faq.question: Is standing at my desk equivalent to walking?
faq.answer: Not for the acute cardiometabolic outcomes reviewed here. In the 2026 Vanherle review, standing-only interventions did not show the same acute benefits as actual physical activity. Standing can still change posture or make movement easier, but Brali does not present it as a metabolic substitute for walking.

intro.html: A walking meeting is useful for a boring reason: it can turn time you were going to spend sitting into time you spend moving. The calendar invite is not a metabolic pathway. The reviewed evidence supports the movement part, while the meeting format is simply one low-friction way to fit it into a workday.

sections.title: 1. Pick a meeting that can travel
sections.html: Start with a conversation that does not need live spreadsheets, detailed visual review or constant note-taking. A one-to-one, routine catch-up, listening call or exploratory conversation is usually easier to move than a screen-share session. If walking would make the work worse, sit. The protocol is replacing avoidable sitting, not collecting steps at the expense of the meeting.

sections.title: 2. Make the smallest useful swap
sections.html: Walk for whatever portion of the meeting is easy to do safely. You do not need a step target, heart-rate zone or heroic route. If you want a starting boundary, use one ordinary screen-free meeting or part of one, then judge whether the format is worth repeating.

sections.title: 3. If the goal is to break sitting, actually move
sections.html:
Two 2026 systematic reviews strengthen the acute metabolic case for physical-activity breaks during prolonged sitting. Vanherle and colleagues synthesized 144 randomized studies and found favourable acute effects on glucose, insulin and blood pressure across activity interventions; standing on its own did not show the same cardiometabolic signal. Gale and colleagues likewise found that activity breaks reduced post-meal glucose and insulin responses, with walking producing the clearest signal among the modes they compared.

That does not mean every meeting needs laps around the building. It means that if you are choosing between another uninterrupted sitting block and a safe bit of walking, the evidence now gives the movement option a more defensible reason than vague advice to ‘move more.’

sections.title: 4. The mechanism is ordinary muscle work
sections.html: The useful mechanism does not require neuroscience confetti. Contracting skeletal muscle uses glucose, and the Vanherle review discusses contraction-driven glucose uptake as one explanation for the acute effect of frequent light-to-moderate activity. The strongest evidence here is still the measured short-term metabolic response, not a promise about energy, mood or productivity.

sections.title: 5. Watch whether the format earns a repeat
sections.html: After the meeting, ask three things: did I replace a meaningful sitting block, did the conversation still work, and was the route safe and practical? Those are better day-to-day signals than chasing a magic step count. If walking makes you miss details, creates confidentiality problems, or competes with traffic and navigation, change the meeting type or use another movement break.

sections.title: 6. Where the evidence stops
sections.html:
The 2026 reviews are strong for an acute question and weak for a long-term promise. Vanherle et al. included randomized controlled studies but emphasized that most evidence came from controlled acute experiments and should not be assumed to produce long-term clinical improvements. Gale et al. included laboratory randomized crossover trials shorter than 24 hours; their studies were small on average and heterogeneous. Neither review tested ‘walking meetings’ as a distinct intervention.

So Brali supports a bounded experiment: use an easy walk to interrupt a long sitting block when the meeting allows it. It does not prescribe a universal 20-minute timer, claim that standing is equivalent, or present walking meetings as treatment for diabetes, hypertension or any other condition.
